questions.stem: A newborn's umbilical cord is inspected after birth. Which finding is expected?
questions.rationale: AVA = Artery–Vein–Artery. The two arteries carry deoxygenated blood and waste away from the fetus, and the one vein carries oxygenated blood to the fetus. Wharton's jelly cushions the vessels.

questions.stem: Which fetal shunt connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing the lungs?
questions.rationale: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary artery to the aorta. The foramen ovale connects the right and left atria, also bypassing the lungs. The ductus venosus bypasses the liver.

questions.stem: Which placental hormone is the basis for most pregnancy tests?
questions.rationale: hCG keeps the corpus luteum making estrogen and progesterone. It's detectable in maternal blood at implantation, about 7–9 days after fertilization. hPL decreases maternal insulin sensitivity.

questions.stem: A patient's last menstrual period began on March 10, 2026. Using Nägele's rule, what is the estimated date of birth?
questions.rationale: March 10 + 7 days = March 17. Going back 3 months gives December 17. That still falls in 2026, so the year doesn't change: December 17, 2026.

questions.stem: A patient is pregnant for the 3rd time. She had twins at 36 weeks (both living) and one miscarriage at 10 weeks. What is her GTPAL?
questions.rationale: G3: this is her 3rd pregnancy. T0: no births at 37 weeks or later. P1: the twins count as one preterm birth (20 to under 37 weeks). A1: the 10-week loss. L2: two living children.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a POSITIVE sign of pregnancy?
options: Fetal movement felt by the examiner
questions.rationale: Positive signs are an audible fetal heartbeat, fetal movement felt by the examiner, and ultrasound visualization. A pregnancy test and Chadwick sign are probable signs. Quickening is presumptive because the patient feels it.

questions.stem: Why should the nurse encourage side-lying (preferably left) rest in the third trimester?
questions.rationale: Lying flat lets the uterus compress the inferior vena cava, reducing return to the heart and risking fetal hypoxia. “Left is best.”

questions.stem: A patient at 34 weeks reports sudden, painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding. Which action should the nurse AVOID?
options: Preparing for a possible Caesarean birth
questions.rationale: Painless bright-red bleeding suggests placenta previa, where the placenta lies over or near the cervix. A vaginal exam could cause hemorrhage. The other actions are all appropriate.

questions.stem: A patient receiving magnesium sulphate for severe pre-eclampsia has absent deep tendon reflexes and a respiratory rate of 10. Which medication should be available?
questions.rationale: These are signs of magnesium toxicity. Calcium gluconate reverses the effects of magnesium sulphate. Naloxone reverses opioids, not magnesium.

questions.stem: When should Rh immune globulin be given to an Rh-negative pregnant patient?
options: At 28 weeks and within 72 hours of birth of an Rh-positive infant
At 20 weeks and within 7 days of birth
Only if the infant is Rh-negative
At the first prenatal visit only
questions.rationale: RhIG is given at 28 weeks and within 72 hours of birth of an Rh-positive infant. It's also given after amniocentesis, a miscarriage or abortion, and abdominal trauma.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected ectopic pregnancy suddenly reports severe lower abdominal pain and right shoulder pain. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Sudden severe pain with referred shoulder pain suggests rupture. Watch for hypovolemic shock: rising weak pulse, falling BP, urine output under 30 mL/h, and cold, clammy skin.

questions.stem: On the fetal monitor, the nurse sees late decelerations. Using VEAL CHOP, what is the most likely cause?
questions.rationale: Variable = Cord compression, Early = Head compression, Accelerations = OK, Late = Placental insufficiency. Improve oxygenation: change position, decrease or stop oxytocin, increase IV fluids, give O₂, and notify the HCP.

questions.stem: Which finding should the nurse report to the health care provider immediately?
questions.rationale: Report more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes, contractions lasting over 90 seconds, a firm resting tone, or less than 30 seconds of rest between contractions.

questions.stem: Which finding is characteristic of TRUE labour rather than prelabour?
options: Discomfort felt mainly in the abdomen and groin
questions.rationale: True labour causes progressive cervical change. Its contractions get stronger with walking and often start in the lower back. Prelabour contractions ease with walking and cause no cervical change.

questions.stem: A labouring patient reports tingling hands and numbness around the mouth during breathing exercises. What should the nurse do?
options: Have her breathe into cupped hands and slow her exhalation
Have her hold her breath while pushing
questions.rationale: These are signs of hyperventilation. Slow the breathing (especially exhalation), breathe into cupped hands or a paper bag, or hold the breath a few seconds before exhaling.

questions.stem: A postpartum patient who had an epidural has a fundus that is high and displaced to the right. What is the priority action?
options: Apply a cold pack to the abdomen
questions.rationale: Epidurals cause urinary retention. A full bladder displaces the uterus and increases the risk of postpartum hemorrhage. Check the bladder and help her void, or catheterize.

questions.stem: Immediately after an amniotomy, the fetal heart rate drops to 90 bpm. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: An FHR outside 110–160 bpm after an amniotomy suggests cord prolapse. Other complications are infection (temperature of 38 °C or higher) and placental abruption. Green fluid means meconium.

questions.stem: A patient on an oxytocin infusion develops uterine tachysystole. What is the nurse's FIRST action?
options: Increase the oxytocin to finish labour faster
Stop the oxytocin or decrease it by half
questions.rationale: Stop or halve the oxytocin. Then increase the mainline IV fluids, reposition (not supine), give O₂ at 8–10 L/min by face mask if SpO₂ is under 96%, and notify the HCP.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of tocolytic therapy in preterm labour?
options: To delay birth long enough to give corticosteroids that mature the fetal lungs
questions.rationale: Tocolytics (e.g., nifedipine first-line) stop contractions long enough to give 1–2 doses of steroids 24–48 hours before birth, so the fetal lungs can mature.

questions.stem: Which is a CONTRAINDICATION to labour induction?
questions.rationale: Contraindications include placenta previa, cord prolapse, abnormal lie, active genital herpes, a previous classical C/S incision, and previous uterine rupture. The other three options are indications for induction.

questions.stem: Where does fertilization normally take place?
options: In the outer third of the fallopian tube
On the surface of the ovary
questions.rationale: Fertilization occurs in the outer third of the fallopian tube, near the ovary. The zygote then travels to the uterus, arriving around day 3, and implants in the upper posterior uterine wall.

questions.stem: Which germ layer develops into the nervous system, skin, hair and nails?
questions.rationale: Ectoderm forms the skin, hair, nails, nervous system and tooth enamel. Mesoderm forms bones, muscles, heart, blood vessels and kidneys. Endoderm forms the linings of the GI and respiratory tracts, plus the liver and pancreas.

questions.stem: Which placental hormone decreases maternal insulin sensitivity so more glucose is available for the fetus?
questions.rationale: hPL decreases maternal insulin sensitivity and glucose use, which helps explain gestational diabetes. Progesterone reduces uterine contractions. hCG keeps the corpus luteum active.

questions.stem: Which is NOT a function of amniotic fluid?
options: Allows fetal movement and symmetrical growth
questions.rationale: Oxygen comes through the placenta and umbilical vein, not the amniotic fluid. Amniotic fluid keeps the temperature constant, cushions the fetus and cord, acts as a barrier to infection, and allows movement and symmetrical growth.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient asks which foods to avoid. Which choice is SAFE?
questions.rationale: Foods to avoid (Box 4.6) carry a Listeria risk: unpasteurized dairy and juices, refrigerated smoked seafood, soft and blue-veined cheeses, deli meats, pâté, and raw or undercooked meat, eggs and seafood. Well-cooked meat is safe.

questions.stem: What is the recommended daily folic acid intake in pregnancy, and why?
options: 0.4 mg, to prevent neural tube defects
questions.rationale: Folic acid 0.4 mg/day (more if high risk) prevents neural tube defects. 27 mg is the iron recommendation, 1000 mg is calcium, and 71 g is protein.

questions.stem: Which vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy?
questions.rationale: Live virus vaccines like MMR are contraindicated, and pregnancy should be avoided for 1 month after MMR. Tdap (after 26 weeks), influenza and COVID-19 are recommended.

questions.stem: A patient at 18 weeks reports she has started feeling the baby move. What is this called, and what type of sign is it?
questions.rationale: Quickening is the first fetal movement felt by the pregnant person, so it's presumptive. Movement felt by the examiner is a positive sign.

questions.stem: Why should a pregnant patient avoid hot tubs and overheating, especially in the first trimester?
questions.rationale: A raised core temperature early in pregnancy is linked to neural tube defects. Exercise is encouraged (150 min/week), but patients should avoid overheating and drink extra fluids.

questions.stem: A patient at 32 weeks has dark-red vaginal bleeding, abdominal pain and a rigid, board-like uterus. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Placental abruption causes painful dark-red bleeding and a tender, rigid uterus. Watch for DIC and hemorrhage, and prepare for an immediate C/S. Previa is painless and bright red.

questions.stem: HELLP syndrome stands for:
options: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets
questions.rationale: HELLP is a severe complication of pre-eclampsia: Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets.

questions.stem: A 50 g glucose challenge test at 26 weeks results in 8.4 mmol/L. What is the next step?
options: No action; the result is normal
questions.rationale: A result above 7.8 mmol/L needs further testing with a 3-hour glucose tolerance test. One abnormal result on that test is diagnostic for GDM.

questions.stem: A newborn's mother is hepatitis B positive. What should the infant receive, and when?
options: Nothing until the infant is tested
Hep B immune globulin and hep B vaccine within 12 hours of birth
Hep B vaccine only, at 2 months
questions.rationale: Infants of HBsAg-positive mothers get hepatitis B immune globulin plus the hep B vaccine within 12 hours of birth.

questions.stem: Which instruction is appropriate for an HIV-positive mother living in Canada?
options: Pump and discard milk for 2 weeks, then breastfeed
Breastfeed only if the viral load is undetectable
questions.rationale: HIV can pass through breast milk, so breastfeeding is not recommended in industrialized countries. With treatment and no breastfeeding, transmission is under 1%.

questions.stem: At 1 minute, a newborn has HR 110, a weak cry, some flexion, a grimace with suction, and a pink body with blue extremities. What is the Apgar score?
questions.rationale: HR over 100 = 2. Weak cry/slow respirations = 1. Some flexion = 1. Grimace = 1. Pink body with blue extremities = 1. Total: 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6. A score of 7–10 is normal, so this baby needs some help.

questions.stem: After the membranes rupture, the nurse notes green-tinged amniotic fluid. What does this suggest?
questions.rationale: Normal amniotic fluid is clear with white flecks of vernix. Green fluid means meconium, which can signal fetal compromise. A foul odour suggests infection.

questions.stem: A perineal tear extends through the anal sphincter into the rectal mucosa. What degree is it?
questions.rationale: First degree: skin or mucosa. Second: deeper perineal tissue. Third: includes the anal sphincter. Fourth: through the sphincter into the rectal mucosa.

questions.stem: A labouring patient has intense back pain. The fetus is occiput posterior. Which position might help?
options: Hands and knees with pelvic rocking
questions.rationale: OP position causes back labour. Hands and knees with pelvic rocking, leaning forward, side-lying, or lunging can help the fetus rotate. Supine is not beneficial.

questions.stem: Why is vitamin K given IM to the newborn within 6 hours of birth?
questions.rationale: Vitamin K (AquaMEPHYTON) helps blood clotting. Erythromycin eye ointment prevents ophthalmia neonatorum.

questions.stem: Which childbirth method is based on breaking the fear–tension–pain cycle?
questions.rationale: Dick-Read focuses on the fear–tension–pain cycle. Bradley is partner-coached childbirth. Lamaze promotes the Healthy Birth Practices.

questions.stem: Shortly after an epidural is started, the patient's BP drops to 88/50. What is the expected first intervention?
options: Increase IV fluids and turn the patient to her side
questions.rationale: Maternal hypotension is a common adverse effect of an epidural. An IV is required to counter it: increase fluids, turn her to the side (avoid supine), and notify the anaesthetist.

questions.stem: Opioids given in labour can cause respiratory depression in the newborn. Which drug reverses it?
questions.rationale: Naloxone reverses opioid respiratory depression. Give the smallest opioid dose that relieves pain to reduce the risk.

questions.stem: What is the difference between induction and augmentation of labour?
options: Induction starts labour; augmentation stimulates contractions already started
Induction uses oxytocin; augmentation uses prostaglandins
Induction is for preterm birth; augmentation is for term birth
questions.rationale: Induction starts labour before it begins naturally. Augmentation stimulates contractions after labour has begun naturally.

questions.stem: Indomethacin used as a tocolytic is limited to 48–72 hours before 32 weeks. Why?
options: It can close the fetal ductus arteriosus too early
questions.rationale: Indomethacin (a prostaglandin inhibitor) can cause premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus. Terbutaline causes maternal tachycardia, and oxytocin can cause water intoxication.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of Cervidil (prostaglandin E₂)?
questions.rationale: Cervidil is given intravaginally as a sustained release to ripen the cervix. A key adverse effect of prostaglandins is uterine tachysystole.

questions.stem: During which period of development is the developing baby called an embryo?
questions.rationale: Zygote: the cell formed at fertilization. Embryo: week 2 to week 8. Fetus: week 9 until birth. The embryonic period is when organs form, so it's the most vulnerable time for teratogens.

questions.stem: A patient asks how long sperm can survive after intercourse. What should the nurse teach?
questions.rationale: Sperm can survive up to 7 days near the cervix, so pregnancy can result from intercourse up to 5 days before ovulation.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the yolk sac?
options: Forms the fetal portion of the placenta
Starts red blood cell production until the fetal liver takes over
questions.rationale: The yolk sac forms on day 9 and starts red blood cell production until the fetal liver takes over around 6 weeks. The chorion forms the fetal portion of the placenta.

questions.stem: Identical (monozygotic) twins develop from:
options: One ovum fertilized by two sperm
Two ova fertilized by two sperm
Two ova fertilized by one sperm
questions.rationale: Monozygotic (identical) twins come from one fertilized ovum that splits. Dizygotic (fraternal) twins come from two separately fertilized ova.

questions.stem: A healthy patient at 32 weeks with an uncomplicated pregnancy asks how often she'll be seen. What does the nurse say?
questions.rationale: Up to 28 weeks: every 4 weeks. 29–36 weeks: every 2–3 weeks. 37 weeks to birth: weekly.

questions.stem: On a routine urinalysis at 30 weeks, the nurse finds protein in the urine. Which condition should the nurse be concerned about?
questions.rationale: Protein in the urine may indicate pre-eclampsia. Ketones can signal inadequate intake, as in hyperemesis. Urine is checked at every prenatal visit.

questions.stem: By about how much does maternal blood volume increase during pregnancy?
questions.rationale: Blood volume rises about 40–50% (~1500 mL). This causes dilutional anemia and provides a reserve for blood loss at birth. Heart rate rises 10–15 bpm, and BP stays about the same.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old pregnant patient needs extra emphasis on which nutrient?
questions.rationale: Teens need 1300 mg/day of calcium (adults 1000 mg), because their own bones are still growing. Pregnant adolescents also face two stressful transitions at once.

questions.stem: Which finding distinguishes hyperemesis gravidarum from normal morning sickness?
options: Weight loss of more than 5% of pre-pregnancy weight
questions.rationale: Hyperemesis is persistent, severe vomiting that starts before 16 weeks, with weight loss over 5% and an inability to eat and drink normally. It may need IV fluids, antiemetics or TPN.

questions.stem: A patient with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy is to receive medication instead of surgery. Which drug is used?
questions.rationale: Methotrexate stops cell division of the pregnancy tissue. Other options are watchful waiting or surgery. The priority is always to control bleeding.

questions.stem: Which blood pressure reading meets the criteria for SEVERE pre-eclampsia?
questions.rationale: Severe: 160/110 or higher on two readings 15 minutes apart. Non-severe: 140/90 or higher on two readings 15 minutes apart, with proteinuria and possible adverse conditions.

questions.stem: Which patient is the best candidate for low-dose aspirin, started at 12–14 weeks?
options: A patient with a history of pre-eclampsia
questions.rationale: Low-dose aspirin starting at 12–14 weeks is recommended for patients at high risk of pre-eclampsia, such as those who had it in a previous pregnancy.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient has active genital herpes lesions when labour begins. What is the plan of care?
options: Isolate the infant from the mother for 2 weeks
questions.rationale: Active genital lesions mean a Caesarean birth to avoid newborn infection. After birth, avoid contact with lesions; isolation isn't needed, and breastfeeding is fine if there are no breast lesions.

questions.stem: A patient who is bleeding heavily has a urine output of 20 mL/h. What does this suggest?
questions.rationale: Urine output under 30 mL/h is a sign of hypovolemic shock, along with a rising weak pulse, falling BP, a rising respiratory rate, and pale, cold, clammy skin.

questions.stem: A patient at 38 weeks says she can breathe more easily but now has to urinate more often. What has most likely happened?
questions.rationale: Lightening is when the fetus descends into the pelvis. It relieves pressure on the diaphragm but increases bladder pressure. It's one of the signs of impending labour.

questions.stem: On the fetal monitor, decelerations mirror each contraction, starting and ending with it. What is the cause, and what action is needed?
questions.rationale: Early decelerations come from head compression. They're expected and need no intervention. VEAL CHOP: Variable = Cord, Early = Head, Accelerations = OK, Late = Placental insufficiency.

questions.stem: How can an anxious, fearful labouring patient's psyche affect labour?
options: It has no effect on labour
Catecholamines inhibit contractions and reduce blood flow to the placenta
questions.rationale: Fear and anxiety release catecholamines, which inhibit uterine contractions and divert blood flow from the placenta. A relaxed, supported patient copes better.

questions.stem: Which pelvis type is most favourable for vaginal birth?
questions.rationale: The gynecoid (round, typical female) pelvis is most favourable. Android (heart-shaped) and platypelloid (flat) are less favourable. Anthropoid is oval and often linked to OP births.

questions.stem: A patient attempting a trial of labour after Caesarean (TOLAC) reports sudden severe lower abdominal pain, and the FHR becomes abnormal. What does the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: The main TOLAC risk is uterine scar rupture. It can disrupt placental blood flow and cause hemorrhage. Signs are severe lower abdominal pain and an abnormal FHR.

questions.stem: Why does the nurse teach open-glottis pushing (blowing out or exhaling while pushing)?
options: To reduce the urge to push
questions.rationale: Panting or blowing out keeps the glottis open and prevents prolonged breath-holding (Valsalva) during pushing, which supports maternal and fetal oxygenation.

questions.stem: A patient who had an epidural develops a severe headache that worsens when she sits up. What treatment may be done?
options: Apply heat to the lower back
questions.rationale: A postdural puncture headache comes from a spinal fluid leak. An epidural blood patch (10–15 mL of her own blood injected into the epidural space) seals the leak.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an analgesic and an anesthetic?
options: An analgesic is always given IV; an anesthetic is always inhaled
An analgesic blocks movement; an anesthetic blocks pain only
An analgesic blocks pain; an anesthetic blocks pain and motor responses
questions.rationale: An analgesic blocks pain only. An anesthetic blocks both pain and motor responses. Regional anesthesia means loss of sensation in an area; general means loss of consciousness and sensation.

questions.stem: After an amniotomy, the patient's temperature is 38.2 °C. What does this suggest?
questions.rationale: A temperature of 38 °C or higher after amniotomy suggests infection. Also watch the FHR (outside 110–160 suggests cord prolapse) and the fluid's colour, odour and amount.

questions.stem: Which is a complication of oxytocin infusion?
options: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
questions.rationale: Oxytocin complications: water intoxication, uterine tachysystole, uterine rupture. It's a high-alert drug given by infusion pump on a secondary line, with continuous fetal monitoring.

questions.stem: Which tocolytic is commonly used as the first-line oral agent?
questions.rationale: Nifedipine (a calcium channel blocker) is first-line oral because it lowers neonatal risks and has a favourable side-effect profile. Terbutaline causes maternal tachycardia, and indomethacin can close the ductus arteriosus.

questions.stem: A precipitous labour is a birth completed in less than:
questions.rationale: Precipitous labour is a birth in under 3 hours. Risks include uterine rupture, cervical lacerations, fetal hypoxia, and birth injury such as intracranial hemorrhage.

questions.stem: What is Chadwick sign?
options: Softening of the lower uterine segment
Bluish-purple colour of the cervix, vagina and vulva
questions.rationale: Chadwick sign is the bluish-purple colour of the cervix, vagina and vulva caused by increased blood supply. It's a probable sign.

questions.stem: What is Goodell sign?
options: First fetal movement felt by the mother
questions.rationale: Goodell sign is softening of the cervix. It's a probable sign.

questions.stem: What is Hegar sign?
options: Softening of the lower uterine segment (isthmus)
questions.rationale: Hegar sign is softening of the lower uterine segment, just above the cervix. It's a probable sign.

questions.stem: On exam, the nurse practitioner notes the cervix is soft. Which sign is this, and how is it classified?
questions.rationale: A soft cervix is Goodell sign. All the eponymous signs (Goodell, Chadwick, Hegar, McDonald) are probable, because the examiner finds them but something other than pregnancy could cause them.

questions.stem: Bluish discoloration of the vaginal mucosa is noted. Which sign is this?
questions.rationale: Bluish discoloration of the cervix, vagina or vulva is Chadwick sign. Estrogen-driven increased blood supply causes it.

questions.stem: Which sign of pregnancy describes being able to flex the uterus easily against the cervix?
questions.rationale: McDonald sign is when the uterus can be easily flexed against the cervix. It's a probable sign listed with Goodell, Chadwick and Hegar on the slides.

questions.stem: Which is a PRESUMPTIVE sign of pregnancy?
questions.rationale: Presumptive signs are what the patient reports: amenorrhea, nausea, breast tenderness, fatigue, urinary frequency, quickening. A pregnancy test and Chadwick sign are probable. Ultrasound is positive.

questions.stem: Why is a positive pregnancy test only a PROBABLE sign, not positive?
options: It is felt by the patient
It is only accurate after 20 weeks
It detects hCG, which can occasionally be present without a viable pregnancy
questions.rationale: Probable signs can have other causes. Pregnancy tests detect hCG, which can occur in conditions other than a normal pregnancy. Only signs from the fetus itself (heartbeat, movement felt by the examiner, ultrasound) are positive.

questions.stem: Which set lists only POSITIVE signs of pregnancy?
options: Fetal heartbeat, movement felt by examiner, ultrasound of fetus
questions.rationale: Positive signs come directly from the fetus: audible fetal heartbeat, fetal movement felt by the examiner, and ultrasound visualization.

questions.stem: Quickening is:
options: Descent of the fetus into the pelvis
Rapid fetal heart rate, a probable sign
The first fetal movement felt by the pregnant person, a presumptive sign
Fetal movement felt by the examiner, a positive sign
questions.rationale: Quickening is the first fetal movement felt by the pregnant person, so it's presumptive. Movement felt by the examiner is positive. Descent into the pelvis is lightening.

questions.stem: Fetal movement is a presumptive sign when felt by ____, but a positive sign when felt by ____.
questions.rationale: Who feels it decides the category. Felt by the patient = presumptive (quickening). Felt by the examiner = positive.

questions.stem: During a vaginal exam, the examiner taps the cervix and the fetus floats up and rebounds. What is this called?
questions.rationale: Ballottement is when the fetus rebounds after a tap on the cervix or lower uterus. It's a probable sign.

questions.stem: How are Braxton Hicks contractions classified, and what are they like?
options: Presumptive; felt only in the third trimester
questions.rationale: Braxton Hicks contractions are irregular, usually painless contractions that don't dilate the cervix. They're a probable sign.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a probable sign of pregnancy?
questions.rationale: Urinary frequency is presumptive because the patient reports it. Hegar sign, abdominal enlargement and fetal outline by palpation are probable signs found by the examiner.

questions.stem: Match the sign: softening of the CERVIX vs. softening of the LOWER UTERINE SEGMENT.
questions.rationale: Goodell = soft cervix. Hegar = soft lower uterine segment (higher up). Chadwick = colour change.

questions.stem: The slides list five early eponymous signs: Chadwick, Ladin, Piskacek, Hegar, and which other?
questions.rationale: The five are Chadwick, Ladin, Piskacek, Hegar and Goodell. Leopold's are palpation maneuvers, Nägele's is the due-date rule, and Apgar scores the newborn.

questions.stem: The period during birth is called:
questions.rationale: Preconception = before pregnancy; antepartum = before birth (prenatal); intrapartum = during birth; postpartum = after birth [slide 4].

questions.stem: What is the main goal of preconception care?
options: Ensuring a person considering pregnancy is in optimal health
questions.rationale: Preconception care aims for optimal health before pregnancy, including a reproductive health plan and assessing social determinants of health [slide 5].

questions.stem: Which social determinant is specifically assessed in preconception care?
questions.rationale: Poverty, food insecurity, unsafe neighbourhoods, lack of education and inadequate social support [slide 5].

questions.stem: LMP began May 20, 2026. Using Naegele's rule, the EDB is:
questions.rationale: May 20 − 3 months = Feb 20; + 7 days = Feb 27; + 1 year = Feb 27, 2027.

questions.stem: LMP began November 19, 2026. The EDB is:
questions.rationale: November (11) − 3 = August (8); 19 + 7 = 26; August comes after November, so it's next year: Aug 26, 2027.

questions.stem: LMP began June 7, 2026 and ended June 12. The EDB is:
questions.rationale: Always use the FIRST day of the LMP. June 7 − 3 months = Mar 7; + 7 days = Mar 14, 2027. The end date is a distractor.

questions.stem: Naegele's rule assumes:
questions.rationale: It assumes a regular 28-day cycle, so it's an estimate. A first-trimester dating ultrasound (after 7 weeks) should be offered when possible [slide 7].

questions.stem: An average pregnancy lasts:
options: 40 weeks (280 days), plus or minus 2 weeks
questions.rationale: 40 weeks (280 days) from the first day of the LMP, plus or minus 2 weeks [slide 7].

questions.stem: The second trimester covers:
questions.rationale: Trimester 1: weeks 1–13. Trimester 2: weeks 14–26. Trimester 3: week 27 to term [slide 9].

questions.stem: For an uncomplicated pregnancy, how often are prenatal visits from conception to 28 weeks?
questions.rationale: Conception–28 weeks: every 4 weeks. 29–36 weeks: every 2–3 weeks. 37 weeks to birth: weekly [slide 15].

questions.stem: A patient at 38 weeks should have prenatal visits:
questions.rationale: From 37 weeks to birth, visits are weekly [slide 15].

questions.stem: About how many prenatal visits are typical in a pregnancy?
questions.rationale: 7–11 visits, though no research supports an optimal number. More are added if complications arise [slide 10].

questions.stem: At what point in pregnancy is blood glucose screening done?
questions.rationale: Blood glucose screening is done between 24 and 28 weeks [slide 14].

questions.stem: The fetal anatomy ultrasound is done at:
questions.rationale: Fetal anatomy ultrasound: 18–22 weeks. Nuchal translucency and multiple marker screening: 11–14 weeks [slide 13].

questions.stem: Leopold's manoeuvres are used at prenatal visits to assess:
questions.rationale: Leopold's manoeuvres = abdominal palpation to find presentation and position. Fundal height tracks fetal growth [slide 14].

questions.stem: Which is checked at EVERY routine prenatal visit?
questions.rationale: Every visit: risk factors, vital signs and weight, urinalysis (protein, ketones), fundal height, Leopold's, FHR, fetal movement, mental health, discomforts [slide 14].

questions.stem: Which is part of the psychosocial history in a prenatal assessment?
questions.rationale: Psychosocial history includes cultural practices and IPV assessment. The others are separate history components [slide 12].

questions.stem: A woman who has never been pregnant is a:
questions.rationale: Nulligravida = never pregnant. Nullipara = no births past 20 weeks (she could have been pregnant). Primigravida = first pregnancy.

questions.stem: A woman pregnant for the first time is a:
questions.rationale: -gravida counts pregnancies; -para counts births past 20 weeks. First pregnancy = primigravida.

questions.stem: Katie is pregnant for the 4th time. She had one child at 34 weeks, one at 39 weeks, and a miscarriage at 8 weeks. Her GTPAL is:
questions.rationale: G4 (includes current). T1 (39 wk). P1 (34 wk). A1 (8 wk). L2 [slide 19].

questions.stem: Currently pregnant, plus twins born at 36 weeks (both living) and a stillbirth at 24 weeks. GTPAL?
questions.rationale: G3 (current + twins as ONE + stillbirth). T0. P2 (twins = one birth at 36 wk; the 24-wk stillbirth counts). A0 (24 wk is past 20). L2.

questions.stem: A loss at 18 weeks counts in GTPAL as:
questions.rationale: Any loss before 20 weeks = A. After 20 and before 37 weeks = preterm, even if the baby didn't survive.

questions.stem: Quickening is a ___ sign of pregnancy.
questions.rationale: Quickening = first fetal movement felt by the mother. Felt by her and could have other causes = presumptive.

questions.stem: A positive pregnancy test (serum or urine) is a ___ sign.
questions.rationale: Probable, because other conditions can raise hCG. Classic trick question [slide 20].

questions.stem: Which is a POSITIVE sign of pregnancy?
options: Fetal movement felt by the examiner
questions.rationale: Positive signs can only be caused by a fetus: audible fetal heartbeat, fetal movement felt by the examiner, ultrasound visualization [slide 20].

questions.stem: Goodell sign is:
options: Softening of the lower uterine segment
questions.rationale: Goodell = softening of the cervix. Chadwick = bluish colour. Hegar = soft lower uterine segment. Braxton Hicks = practice contractions. All probable signs.

questions.stem: Chadwick sign (bluish-purple cervix and vagina) is classified as:
questions.rationale: Chadwick, Goodell, Hegar, McDonald, Braxton Hicks, ballottement and a positive test are all probable signs [slide 20].

questions.stem: By how much does maternal blood volume increase in pregnancy?
questions.rationale: Blood volume rises about 40–50%, for placental exchange, expanded maternal tissue, and a reserve for blood loss at birth [Part 2, slide 11].

questions.stem: What happens to blood pressure in a normal pregnancy?
questions.rationale: BP remains the same. Pulse rises 10–15 bpm and BMR rises 10–20% [slide 11]. A rising BP points to hypertensive disorders (Ch 5).

questions.stem: Maternal pulse rate typically increases by:
questions.rationale: Pulse increases by 10–15 beats per minute [slide 11].

questions.stem: Physiological (dilutional) anemia in pregnancy happens because:
options: Iron is lost through the placenta
Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass
Blood is lost at each visit
questions.rationale: Blood volume expands faster than red cells, diluting the hemoglobin, so it's called dilutional anemia [slide 13].

questions.stem: Why is the risk of thrombophlebitis higher in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters?
questions.rationale: Clotting factors increase in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters, raising the risk of thrombophlebitis [slide 13].

questions.stem: A pregnant patient lying flat on her back becomes dizzy and lightheaded. What's happening and what's the fix?
options: Supine hypotension from vena cava compression; turn her onto her left side
questions.rationale: Supine hypotension (aortocaval compression): the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava, reducing return to the heart and risking fetal hypoxia. Turn to the side, preferably the left [slide 12].

questions.stem: Why should the nurse encourage side-lying sleep in the third trimester?
questions.rationale: Side-lying prevents supine hypotension [slide 14 question].

questions.stem: Oxygen consumption in pregnancy increases by about:
questions.rationale: O₂ consumption rises 20–40%. Breathing is deeper, but the respiratory rate increases only slightly [slide 10].

questions.stem: A pregnant patient complains of nasal stuffiness and nosebleeds. The cause is:
options: Increased estrogen causing swelling of mucous membranes
questions.rationale: Estrogen causes edema of the nose, pharynx, mouth and trachea mucous membranes, so stuffiness and epistaxis are common [slide 10].

questions.stem: Dyspnea in late pregnancy usually improves after:
questions.rationale: The diaphragm rises about 4 cm, causing dyspnea until the fetus descends into the pelvis (lightening) [slide 10].

questions.stem: Which GI change contributes to constipation and heartburn in pregnancy?
options: Delayed gastric emptying and slower intestinal movement
questions.rationale: Delayed gastric emptying and intestinal movement cause constipation, bloating, hemorrhoids and heartburn. Gastric acid actually decreases [slide 15].

questions.stem: Pregnant patients are more susceptible to which infection?
questions.rationale: Increased susceptibility to UTIs; also more frequent urination in the 1st and 3rd trimesters [slide 17].

questions.stem: The dark line down the middle of the abdomen in pregnancy is called:
questions.rationale: Linea nigra = dark midline. Chloasma = the 'mask of pregnancy' on the face. Striae = stretch marks [slide 18].

questions.stem: Higher vaginal glycogen levels in pregnancy promote:
questions.rationale: Higher glycogen promotes Candida albicans growth [slide 8].

questions.stem: What is the recommended total weight gain for a person with a normal pre-pregnancy BMI (18.5–24.9)?
questions.rationale: Normal BMI: 11.5–16 kg (25–35 lb). Underweight: 12.5–18. Overweight: 7–11.5. Obese: 5–9 [slide 24].

questions.stem: Recommended weight gain in the FIRST trimester is:
questions.rationale: First trimester: 0.5–2.0 kg (1.1–4.4 lb) [slide 23].

questions.stem: Daily protein requirement in pregnancy:
questions.rationale: Protein: 71 g/day [slide 26].

questions.stem: Daily iron requirement in pregnancy:
questions.rationale: Iron: 27 mg/day, which usually requires a multivitamin [slide 26].

questions.stem: Daily folic acid requirement in pregnancy (standard risk):
questions.rationale: Folic acid: 0.4 mg/day, more if high risk for neural tube defects [slide 26].

questions.stem: Daily calcium requirement for a pregnant ADOLESCENT:
questions.rationale: Calcium: 1300 mg/day for teens, 1000 mg/day for adults [slide 26].

questions.stem: Folic acid in pregnancy mainly prevents:
questions.rationale: Folic acid prevents neural tube defects; ideally started before conception.

questions.stem: Which food should a pregnant patient AVOID?
questions.rationale: Avoid refrigerated smoked seafood, uncooked hot dogs, non-dried deli meats, raw/unpasteurized dairy, soft and blue-veined cheeses, raw eggs, raw sprouts, pâté, unpasteurized juice (Box 4.6) [slide 27].

questions.stem: Recommended exercise in pregnancy is:
options: 150 minutes of moderate activity per week over at least 3 days
questions.rationale: 150 min/week of moderate activity, at least 3 days a week, aerobic plus resistance; use the talk test [slide 30].

questions.stem: Why should pregnant patients avoid overheating during exercise?
options: Elevated body temperature is linked to neural tube defects
questions.rationale: Avoid overheating and increase fluids [slide 30]. Textbook: high core temperature, especially in the 1st trimester, is linked to neural tube defects.

questions.stem: Air travel is generally considered safe up to:
questions.rationale: Air travel is generally safe up to 36 weeks; avoid sitting for long periods [slide 35].

questions.stem: The Tdap (whooping cough) vaccine is recommended:
questions.rationale: Tdap after 26 weeks protects the fetus and newborn [slide 36].

questions.stem: How much alcohol is considered safe in pregnancy?
questions.rationale: No amount of alcohol is safe. Risk: fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) [slide 34].

questions.stem: Which is a FIRST-trimester discomfort?
questions.rationale: 1st trimester: nausea, breast tenderness, urinary frequency, nasal stuffiness, epistaxis, leukorrhea, fatigue. The others are 2nd/3rd trimester [slide 38].

questions.stem: A pregnant teen faces which unique psychosocial challenge?
options: Coping with two stress-laden transitions at once: adolescence and parenthood
questions.rationale: The pregnant adolescent copes with two stressful transitions at the same time [slide 41].

questions.stem: A patient discloses that her partner is abusing her. What's the nurse's priority?
options: Keep it strictly confidential and refer to resources; the decision to leave is hers
Document it in front of the partner
questions.rationale: Disclosures must be kept absolutely confidential, since her life may be in danger if the abuser learns of it. Refer to shelters; the decision to leave is her own [slide 40].

questions.stem: Which is a danger sign in pregnancy that should be reported?
options: Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
questions.rationale: Danger signs include decreased or absent fetal movement after 26–28 weeks, bleeding, fluid gush before 37 weeks, severe headache, blurred vision, epigastric pain, face/hand swelling, fever over 37.8 °C [slide 5].

questions.stem: A pregnant patient has a severe headache, blurred vision and epigastric pain. These danger signs most suggest:
questions.rationale: Headache, visual changes, epigastric pain and swelling of the face/hands point to pre-eclampsia.

questions.stem: Hyperemesis gravidarum is defined by persistent vomiting starting before 16 weeks and weight loss of more than:
questions.rationale: More than 5% of pre-pregnancy weight [slide 8].

questions.stem: Priority nursing care for hyperemesis gravidarum:
options: Accurate intake and output; correct dehydration
questions.rationale: Correct dehydration and electrolyte/acid–base imbalance; accurate I&O; avoid triggers; antiemetics; TPN in extreme cases [slides 9–10].

questions.stem: A patient is actively bleeding during a miscarriage. The nurse should:
options: Keep her NPO and monitor vital signs for shock
questions.rationale: If actively bleeding, keep NPO; monitor VS for hypovolemic shock; document bleeding and save clots/tissue [slide 11].

questions.stem: Which is correct discharge teaching after a miscarriage?
options: Pregnancy can occur before the first period returns
questions.rationale: Also: no tampons, temperature every 8 h for 3 days, report bleeding or infection, iron if prescribed [slide 12].

questions.stem: Where do 95% of ectopic pregnancies occur?
questions.rationale: 95% are in the fallopian tube [slide 15].

questions.stem: A patient with a suspected ectopic pregnancy reports new shoulder pain. This suggests:
questions.rationale: Shoulder pain is referred from blood irritating the diaphragm after rupture. Report increasing or shoulder pain [slides 16–17].

questions.stem: Which drug may treat an unruptured ectopic pregnancy by stopping cell division?
questions.rationale: Methotrexate inhibits cell division. Other options: no action, or surgery [slide 17].

questions.stem: Which is a sign of hypovolemic shock?
questions.rationale: Shock: rising weak pulse, rising RR, falling BP, urine under 30 mL/h, pale cold clammy skin, thirst [slide 18].

questions.stem: Painless, bright-red vaginal bleeding in late pregnancy suggests:
questions.rationale: Previa = bright red, painless. Abruption = dark red, painful, with a board-like uterus [slides 20, 22].

questions.stem: Dark-red bleeding with a tender, board-like uterus suggests:
questions.rationale: Abruption: premature separation, dark red bleeding with pain, rigid tender uterus [slides 22–23].

questions.stem: Which is a major predisposing factor for placental abruption?
questions.rationale: Hypertension, cocaine, tobacco, poor nutrition, abdominal trauma, previous abruption [slide 22].

questions.stem: A serious complication of placental abruption that depletes clotting factors is:
questions.rationale: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); also postpartum hemorrhage [slide 24].

questions.stem: Usual treatment for placental abruption:
options: Immediate Caesarean birth; blood and clotting factor replacement
questions.rationale: Immediate C-section with blood and clotting factor replacement [slide 24].

questions.stem: Gestational hypertension is defined as hypertension that begins:
questions.rationale: Chronic HTN exists before pregnancy or before 20 weeks; gestational HTN starts after 20 weeks [slide 28].

questions.stem: BP readings for SEVERE pre-eclampsia:
questions.rationale: Non-severe: ≥140/90. Severe: ≥160/110, two readings 15 minutes apart [slide 30].

questions.stem: Eclampsia is defined by:
questions.rationale: Eclampsia = generalized tonic-clonic seizures; magnesium sulphate is given [slide 28].

questions.stem: Magnesium sulphate is given in pre-eclampsia to:
questions.rationale: Seizure prevention. Antihypertensives treat BP [slide 34].

questions.stem: The antidote for magnesium sulphate toxicity is:
questions.rationale: Calcium gluconate reverses magnesium sulphate [slide 34].

questions.stem: High-risk patients may take low-dose aspirin to prevent pre-eclampsia starting at:
questions.rationale: Low-dose aspirin started between 12 and 14 weeks [slide 32].

questions.stem: Rh incompatibility puts the baby at risk when the:
options: Mother is Rh-positive and baby Rh-negative
Mother is Rh-negative and baby Rh-positive
questions.rationale: An Rh-negative mother makes antibodies against Rh-positive fetal blood; the next pregnancy is at risk of hemolytic disease of the newborn [slide 37].

questions.stem: Rh immune globulin is given at which point in pregnancy?
questions.rationale: At 28 weeks and within 72 h of the birth of an Rh-positive baby; also after amniocentesis, miscarriage/abortion, abdominal trauma [slide 39].

questions.stem: After the birth of an Rh-positive baby, Rh immune globulin must be given within:
questions.rationale: Within 72 hours [slide 39].

questions.stem: GDM screening (glucose challenge test) is done at:
questions.rationale: 24–28 weeks: 50 g challenge, then a 3-h test if over 7.8; one abnormal 3-h value is diagnostic [slide 43].

questions.stem: A newborn of a mother with GDM should be monitored most closely for:
questions.rationale: Hypoglycemia, respiratory distress, and injury from macrosomia [slide 46].

questions.stem: Herpes: when is a Caesarean birth indicated?
options: Active genital lesions at the time of labour
questions.rationale: C-section if active genital lesions are present [slide 50].

questions.stem: A baby born to a hepatitis B–positive mother should receive:
options: Only the hep B vaccine at 2 months
HBIG plus the hep B vaccine within 12 hours of birth
questions.rationale: HBIG plus hep B vaccine within 12 h of birth [slide 51].

questions.stem: Which is correct teaching for an HIV-positive mother in Canada?
questions.rationale: Not recommended to breastfeed in industrialized countries; adequately treated, non-breastfeeding mothers have under 1% transmission [slides 53–54].

questions.stem: Untreated syphilis in pregnancy is treated with:
questions.rationale: Penicillin. Untreated, 70–100% of newborns get congenital syphilis [slide 55].

questions.stem: Ductus venosus: what does it bypass?
questions.rationale: Ductus venosus bypasses the LIVER. Memory hook: venosus → vein → umbilical vein → liver.

questions.stem: Ductus venosus: what is its route?
options: Umbilical vein to inferior vena cava
questions.rationale: Umbilical vein → inferior vena cava, skipping the liver.

questions.stem: Ductus venosus: when does it close?
options: Functionally when the cord is cut; permanently in about 1 week
questions.rationale: Closes when the cord is cut, permanently in about 1 week, then becomes a ligament [slide 42].

questions.stem: Foramen ovale: what is its route?
options: Umbilical vein to inferior vena cava
questions.rationale: Right atrium → left atrium (an opening in the atrial wall), bypassing the lungs.

questions.stem: Foramen ovale: when does it close?
options: Within 15 hours; permanently in about 3 weeks
questions.rationale: Within 2 hours of birth, permanently by age 3 months [slide 42].

questions.stem: Ductus arteriosus: what is its route?
options: Umbilical vein to inferior vena cava
questions.rationale: Pulmonary artery → aorta. Memory hook: arteriosus → arteries → pulmonary artery and aorta.

questions.stem: Ductus arteriosus: when does it close?
options: Within 15 hours; permanently in about 3 weeks
questions.rationale: Within 15 hours, permanently in about 3 weeks [slide 42]. (Ch 8 link: indomethacin can close it too early.)

questions.stem: Which TWO shunts bypass the lungs?
questions.rationale: Foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the lungs. Ductus venosus is the odd one out: it bypasses the liver.

questions.stem: After permanent closure, which shunts become ligaments?
questions.rationale: The two ducts (ductus arteriosus and ductus venosus) become ligaments [slide 42].

questions.stem: Put the shunt closures in order, fastest first:
options: Ductus venosus (cord cut) → foramen ovale (2 h) → ductus arteriosus (15 h)
Foramen ovale → ductus arteriosus → ductus venosus
Ductus arteriosus → foramen ovale → ductus venosus
They all close at the same time
questions.rationale: Cord cut (ductus venosus) → 2 h (foramen ovale) → 15 h (ductus arteriosus). Permanent: 1 week → 3 weeks (DA) → 3 months (FO).

questions.stem: An 8-week-old developing human is called:
questions.rationale: Embryo = weeks 2–8. At week 8 it's still an embryo; it becomes a fetus at week 9.

questions.stem: A 10-week-old developing human is called:
questions.rationale: Fetus = week 9 to birth.

questions.stem: The age of viability (per the slides) is:
questions.rationale: 22 weeks of gestation, with NICU care to survive [slide 23]. Don't confuse it with 20 weeks, the cut-off for abortion vs. preterm in GTPAL.

questions.stem: Which number is the GTPAL cut-off between an abortion and a preterm birth, NOT the age of viability?
questions.rationale: 20 weeks separates abortion from preterm in GTPAL (Ch 4). Viability is 22 weeks. Term is 37 weeks or more.

questions.stem: Approximate amniotic fluid volume at 20 weeks:
questions.rationale: About 30 mL at 10 weeks → 350 mL at 20 weeks → 700–1000 mL at 37 weeks [slide 17].

questions.stem: Approximate amniotic fluid volume at 37 weeks:
questions.rationale: 700–1000 mL at 37 weeks. Over 1000 mL at term = polyhydramnios (per the slides).

questions.stem: hCG is detectable in maternal blood how soon after fertilization?
questions.rationale: As soon as implantation occurs, usually 7–9 days after fertilization [slide 32].

questions.stem: Which is NOT a function of progesterone in pregnancy?
options: Causes the corpus luteum to persist
questions.rationale: Keeping the corpus luteum going is hCG's job. Progesterone: lining, fewer contractions, breasts, maternal metabolism, male reproductive tract (via testosterone) [slide 30].

questions.stem: Which is a NON-pregnancy effect of estrogen?
questions.rationale: Estrogen side effects: more skin pigment, vascular changes in nose and mouth, more saliva [slide 31].

questions.stem: Match the hormone: makes more glucose available to the fetus.
questions.rationale: hPL decreases maternal insulin sensitivity and glucose use.

questions.stem: When does the morula enter the uterus?
questions.rationale: The morula enters the uterus on the third day, then floats for another 2–4 days [slide 13].

questions.stem: The yolk sac forms on day 9 and makes red blood cells until which organ takes over (around 6 weeks)?
questions.rationale: The yolk sac initiates RBC production until the fetal liver takes over around 6 weeks [slide 20].

questions.stem: The trophoblast (outer blastocyst layer) develops into the:
questions.rationale: Outer layer (trophoblast) → chorion. Inner cell mass → embryo and embryonic membranes [slide 13].

questions.stem: Normal umbilical cord length is about:
questions.rationale: About 55 cm (22 inches); it usually inserts near the centre of the placenta [slide 35].

questions.stem: Sperm can survive up to ___ days, so intercourse up to ___ days before ovulation can result in pregnancy.
questions.rationale: Sperm survive up to 7 days; pregnancy can occur with intercourse up to 5 days before ovulation [slide 10].

questions.stem: Which germ layer gives rise to muscle, bone and the heart?
questions.rationale: Mesoderm (middle): muscle, bone, cartilage, heart and vessels, kidneys, reproductive organs. Ecto = outer (skin, nerves). Endo = inner (GI and respiratory linings).

questions.stem: Twins occur in about 1 in every ___ pregnancies.
questions.rationale: About 1 in 43 pregnancies, more often with fertility drugs [slide 43].

questions.stem: Which parent's gamete determines the biological sex of the baby?
options: The mother's ovum, which carries X or Y
The father's sperm, which carries X or Y
Both contribute equally to sex determination
The placenta determines sex after implantation
questions.rationale: The ovum always carries an X. The sperm carries either an X or a Y, so the sperm decides: XX = female, XY = male [slides 6, 11].

questions.stem: Where does implantation usually occur?
questions.rationale: Implantation usually happens in the upper section of the posterior uterine wall [slide 14].

questions.stem: Body cells contain 46 chromosomes. How many does each gamete (sperm or ovum) contain after meiosis?
questions.rationale: Meiosis produces haploid gametes with 23 chromosomes, including one sex chromosome [slide 6].

questions.stem: Which germ layer develops into the nervous system and skin?
questions.rationale: Ectoderm (outer layer): skin, hair, nails, nervous system, sense organs. Mesoderm: muscle, bone, heart. Endoderm: linings of the GI and respiratory tracts [Box 3.1].

questions.stem: Which germ layer forms the lining of the GI and respiratory tracts?
questions.rationale: Endoderm (inner layer) forms the linings of the GI and respiratory tracts, plus the liver, pancreas, thyroid and bladder [Box 3.1].

questions.stem: A patient has blood drawn to see if she is pregnant. Which hormone is responsible for a positive result?
questions.rationale: hCG is detectable 7–9 days after fertilization and is the basis of pregnancy tests. It keeps the corpus luteum producing estrogen and progesterone [slide 32].

questions.stem: Which placental hormone reduces uterine contractions, helping prevent miscarriage and preterm labour?
questions.rationale: Progesterone maintains the uterine lining and reduces uterine contractions. It also prepares breasts for lactation [slide 30].

questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates uterine growth and increases blood flow to uterine vessels?
questions.rationale: Estrogen stimulates uterine growth, increases uterine blood flow, and develops breast glandular tissue [slide 31].

questions.stem: How many vessels does a normal umbilical cord have, and what do they carry?
options: 1 artery to the fetus, 2 veins away
2 arteries away from the fetus, 1 vein to the fetus
2 arteries to the fetus, 1 vein away
questions.rationale: AVA: 2 arteries carry deoxygenated blood and waste away from the fetus; 1 vein carries oxygenated blood to the fetus [slides 35–36].

questions.stem: What substance covers and cushions the umbilical cord vessels?
questions.rationale: Wharton's jelly covers and cushions the cord vessels [slide 35].

questions.stem: The embryonic stage of development lasts from:
questions.rationale: Zygote = fertilization; embryo = weeks 2–8; fetus = week 9 to birth [slide 23].

questions.stem: According to the slides, the age of viability is:
questions.rationale: Viability is 22 weeks of gestation, but the baby needs NICU care to survive [slide 23].

questions.stem: Amniotic fluid exceeding 1000 mL at term is called:
questions.rationale: Polyhydramnios = too much amniotic fluid. The slides uses over 1000 mL at term. Oligohydramnios = too little [slide 18].

questions.stem: A teratogen is:
options: A hormone produced by the placenta
Anything that can cause birth defects
An enzyme that breaks down amniotic fluid
questions.rationale: A teratogen is any substance or factor that causes birth defects, such as drugs, alcohol, smoking or infection [slide 4].

questions.stem: Which fetal shunt allows blood to bypass the liver?
questions.rationale: The ductus venosus bypasses the liver (umbilical vein to inferior vena cava). The foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus bypass the lungs.

questions.stem: The foramen ovale connects which two structures?
options: Umbilical vein and inferior vena cava
questions.rationale: The foramen ovale shunts blood from the right atrium to the left atrium, bypassing the lungs. It closes within 2 hours of birth [slide 42].

questions.stem: Why does the fetus need shunts that bypass the lungs?
options: The lungs are not yet formed
The fetus gets oxygen from the placenta, not the lungs
questions.rationale: The placenta is the organ of fetal respiration, so most blood can skip the fluid-filled lungs.

questions.stem: Which shunt closes functionally when the umbilical cord is cut?
options: None; they all close at 3 months
questions.rationale: Ductus venosus closes when the cord is cut (permanently in about 1 week). Foramen ovale: within 2 h. Ductus arteriosus: within 15 h [slide 42].

questions.stem: Identical twins are:
options: Monozygotic, from a single fertilized ovum
Dizygotic, from one ovum and two sperm
Always the result of fertility drugs
questions.rationale: Monozygotic = one fertilized ovum = identical. Dizygotic = two ova = fraternal [slide 43].

questions.stem: Which is a concern related to multifetal pregnancy?
options: Uterine overdistention increasing the risk of preterm labour
questions.rationale: Textbook: overdistention raises the risk of preterm labour and postpartum hemorrhage; shared placental nutrition raises the risk of growth restriction and anemia.

questions.stem: Oxytocin is running and the patient has 6 contractions in 10 minutes. First action?
options: Stop the oxytocin or cut it by half
questions.rationale: This is tachysystole. Stop or halve the oxytocin, increase the mainline IV, reposition off the back, give O2 at 8–10 L/min if SpO2 is under 96%, and notify the provider.

questions.stem: Most common UTERINE incision for a Caesarean?
questions.rationale: Low transverse is the most common uterine incision. Pfannenstiel (transverse) is the most common skin incision.

questions.stem: The fundus is high and pushed to the right. First action?
questions.rationale: A full bladder displaces the uterus and can lead to PPH.

questions.stem: Lochia serosa begins around:
questions.rationale: Rubra comes first, then serosa from day 4 (lasting 2–4 weeks), then alba (yellow/clear) until 4–6 weeks.

questions.stem: Bright red trickle of blood with a FIRM fundus suggests:
questions.rationale: A firm uterus with bright red, continuous bleeding points to trauma (a laceration).

questions.stem: Perineum care in the first 24 hours:
questions.rationale: Cold for the first 24 hours reduces swelling. After that, heat (sitz bath) increases blood flow.

questions.stem: Best Rubin phase for teaching:
questions.rationale: In taking-hold the patient is more independent and eager to learn. Taking-in is the dependent, retelling-the-birth phase.

questions.stem: Prolactin vs oxytocin — which is correct?
questions.rationale: Prolactin makes milk. Oxytocin causes let-down and uterine contractions (afterpains).

questions.stem: Late hunger cue?
questions.rationale: Crying is a late hunger cue.

questions.stem: Breast milk in the fridge at 4°C is good for:
questions.rationale: Fridge 96 hours, room temperature 4 hours, freezer 6–12 months. Never microwave it.

questions.stem: Most common cause of PPH?
questions.rationale: Tone (uterine atony) is the most common of the 4 T's.

questions.stem: First sign of hypovolemic shock?
questions.rationale: Tachycardia comes first. Suspect shock if the postpartum pulse is over 100. Low BP is late.

questions.stem: Mastitis — should she keep breastfeeding?
options: Only from the unaffected side, forever
Switch to formula until the antibiotics finish
questions.rationale: Keep emptying the breast. Treat with antibiotics, heat, fluids and rest.

questions.stem: Postpartum infection temperature criterion:
options: ≥ 38°C after the first 24 h, on 2 days within the first 10 days
questions.rationale: 38°C or higher after the first 24 hours, on at least 2 days within the first 10 days.

questions.stem: Newborn normal HR and RR:
questions.rationale: HR 110–160 (apical, 1 full minute), RR 30–60, temp 36.5–37.5°C axillary.

questions.stem: Swelling that CROSSES suture lines:
questions.rationale: Caput crosses. A cephalohematoma (blood under the periosteum) does not.

questions.stem: Newborn hypoglycemia after 12 hours of age is glucose below:
questions.rationale: Below 2.6 mmol/L after 12 hours (it may be 1.8 in the first hour). Signs: jittery, poor suck, high-pitched cry, low temp.

questions.stem: Jaundice at 20 hours of age is:
questions.rationale: Physiological jaundice appears on days 2–3. In the first 24 hours it is pathological.

questions.stem: Dry, cracked, peeling skin, long nails and little vernix suggest:
questions.rationale: These are post-term features. Preterm babies have thin skin, abundant vernix and lanugo, and few sole creases.

questions.stem: Tremors, high-pitched cry, sneezing and yawning at 30 hours point to:
questions.rationale: NAS/NOWS starts within 24–48 hours. Care: keep mother and baby together, skin-to-skin, swaddle, vertical rocking, quiet room, breastfeeding usually encouraged.

questions.stem: Before starting oxytocin, the cervix must be soft/ripe. Which drug is given to soften it?
questions.rationale: Cervidil (prostaglandin E2, intravaginal, sustained release) softens the cervix. Misoprostol can cause tachysystole.

questions.stem: Oxytocin's water-retaining effect can cause:
questions.rationale: The three oxytocin complications are water intoxication, uterine tachysystole and uterine rupture.

questions.stem: A patient had a classic uterine incision last birth. This pregnancy:
options: A previous classic incision contraindicates induction
questions.rationale: A previous classic incision (or uterine rupture) is a contraindication to induction because of rupture risk.

questions.stem: After the first day, the fundus descends about:
questions.rationale: About 1 cm (one fingerbreadth) per day.

questions.stem: The fundus is boggy. First action?
questions.rationale: Massage until firm (don't over-massage), make sure the bladder is empty, and encourage breastfeeding. Report it if the uterus stays boggy.

questions.stem: Foul-smelling lochia with a fever on day 5 suggests:
questions.rationale: Foul lochia, with or without fever, is a sign of infection.

questions.stem: Lochia rubra that continues past day 4 suggests:
questions.rationale: Rubra past day 4 points to retained placenta. A return to bright red after serosa or alba points to hemorrhage.

questions.stem: In REEDA, the A stands for:
questions.rationale: Redness, Edema, Ecchymosis, Discharge, Approximation (how well the edges meet).

questions.stem: A NON-breastfeeding patient's period usually returns in:
questions.rationale: 6–8 weeks if not breastfeeding. Breastfeeding delays ovulation, usually 6–12 months.

questions.stem: Rh immune globulin is given when:
questions.rationale: Rh-negative parent with an Rh-positive baby. Give the rubella vaccine if she is non-immune.

questions.stem: Adequate intake for a 6-day-old breastfed baby:
questions.rationale: 6–8 wet diapers by day 6, several stools, at least 8 feeds, an audible swallow, and no more than 10% weight loss.

questions.stem: A newborn has lost 12% of birth weight by day 4. The nurse should:
options: Report it; over 10% suggests inadequate intake
questions.rationale: 7–10% loss is expected. More than 10% needs follow-up.

questions.stem: Methylergonovine is ordered for atony. Which finding means hold it and check with the provider?
questions.rationale: Methylergonovine raises BP, so it's avoided in hypertension. Carboprost is avoided in asthma.

questions.stem: Severe perineal pain not relieved by analgesics, with a bulging purplish mass:
questions.rationale: Hematoma. Small ones are treated with ice; large ones need ligation by the provider.

questions.stem: Sudden chest pain, dyspnea and cough postpartum suggest:
questions.rationale: PE. DVT signs are in the leg: calf pain, edema, colour change, and a circumference increase of more than 2 cm.

questions.stem: At 1 week she hears voices saying the baby isn't hers. Priority?
options: Treat as a medical emergency; keep mother and baby safe
questions.rationale: Hallucinations and delusions point to perinatal psychosis, a medical emergency.

questions.stem: A newborn placed on a cold scale loses heat by:
questions.rationale: Conduction is direct contact with a cold surface. Radiation is heat lost to nearby cold objects not touching the baby.

questions.stem: Startled newborn throws arms out, palms up:
questions.rationale: Moro reflex. The slide notes say it stops around 6 months; rooting stops around 4 months.

questions.stem: The Ballard score is used to:
questions.rationale: Ballard estimates gestational age from physical and neuromuscular signs. Rating condition at 1 and 5 minutes is the Apgar.

questions.stem: Which statement about PKU is correct?
options: Can't process phenylalanine; screened at 24–48 h
questions.rationale: PKU is autosomal recessive. It's found by newborn screening at 24–48 h and managed with a careful diet, frequent blood phe checks and sapropterin.

questions.stem: How is oxytocin given for induction?
options: On a secondary IV line through an infusion pump, with continuous fetal monitoring
questions.rationale: It's a high-alert drug: secondary line, infusion pump, titrated, continuous EFM. That way it can be stopped right away.

questions.stem: Most common SKIN incision for a Caesarean?
questions.rationale: Pfannenstiel is the most common skin incision. Low transverse is the most common uterine incision.

questions.stem: Why walk early after a Caesarean?
options: Prevents clots and helps bowels start working
questions.rationale: Early ambulation prevents DVT/PE and helps breathing and peristalsis.

questions.stem: In BUBBLLEE, the two L's are:
questions.rationale: Breasts, Uterus, Bladder, Bowel, Lochia, Legs, Episiotomy/laceration/incision, Emotions.

questions.stem: A pad weighs 85 g more than dry. Estimated blood loss?
questions.rationale: 1 g = 1 mL. No more than 1 saturated pad per hour.

questions.stem: Best teaching for a 4th degree laceration:
options: High-fibre diet and plenty of fluids
questions.rationale: This prevents constipation that could break down the sutured area.

questions.stem: She cramps every time she breastfeeds. The nurse explains:
options: Oxytocin release contracts the uterus; this is normal
questions.rationale: Afterpains are normal. Analgesics (usually acetaminophen) help.

questions.stem: No void 6 h after birth and no urge. Try first:
options: Run water and use warm water from the peri-bottle
questions.rationale: Try non-invasive steps first: privacy, don't rush, running water, hands in warm water, peri-bottle. A full bladder can cause PPH.

questions.stem: Day 1: she keeps retelling her birth story and wants help with meals. Rubin phase?
questions.rationale: Taking-in (days 1–2) is dependent and focused on her own needs. Taking-hold is the best time to teach.

questions.stem: Which INFANT condition contraindicates breastfeeding?
questions.rationale: Galactosemia. Parent contraindications include HIV, Ebola, untreated brucellosis, illicit drugs, chemo and radioactive isotopes.

questions.stem: Milk at the END of a feed is:
questions.rationale: Foremilk quenches thirst. Hindmilk has more fat, satisfies the baby and supports weight gain.

questions.stem: Which formula statement is safe?
options: I'll follow the mixing directions exactly
questions.rationale: Over- or under-dilution can cause serious illness. Don't prop the bottle or microwave it.

questions.stem: PPH on day 5 is classified as:
questions.rationale: Early is within 24 h. Late is 24 h to 12 weeks.

questions.stem: Bleeding vaginal laceration. Until the provider assesses her:
questions.rationale: She may need suturing under anesthesia.

questions.stem: Which teaching helps PREVENT puerperal infection?
questions.rationale: Hand hygiene, pads front to back, finish all antibiotics, and watch for signs of infection.

questions.stem: Flat and tearful at 2 weeks. Best action?
options: Screen with a valid depression tool
questions.rationale: Never assume it's baby blues. Screen, and refer if the screen is positive.

questions.stem: 6-hour-old with blue hands and feet, pink lips and trunk:
questions.rationale: Acrocyanosis is normal for the first few weeks. Central cyanosis is not.

questions.stem: A 2-hour-old newborn is sleepy and hard to rouse. Most likely:
questions.rationale: First reactivity is 30–60 min, decreased responsiveness 1–3 h, second reactivity 3–8 h.

questions.stem: Why is a post-term newborn at risk of hypoglycemia?
options: Depleted glycogen from an aging placenta
questions.rationale: Other post-term risks: oligohydramnios, meconium aspiration, polycythemia, difficult birth, seizures.

questions.stem: Which nursing point is specific to Down syndrome?
options: Hypotonia makes holding harder and adds to heat loss
questions.rationale: Hypotonia also raises the risk of respiratory illness and constipation. Phe restriction is for PKU; withdrawal at 24–48 h is NAS.

questions.stem: Which uterine incision is a vertical cut high on the uterus and rules out a future induction?
questions.rationale: Classic. A previous classic incision (or uterine rupture) contraindicates induction because of rupture risk. Pfannenstiel is a skin incision.

questions.stem: Which is a contraindication to Caesarean birth?
questions.rationale: Also a fetus that isn't viable or is too premature to survive. Breech, previa and cord prolapse are indications.

questions.stem: After a Caesarean, catheter urine output is dropping and pulse is rising. Main concern?
questions.rationale: Recovery-room VS and urine output are watched to pick up hemorrhage or shock early.

questions.stem: Day 3: both breasts hard, warm and sore, no fever. Best teaching?
options: Feed often or hand express; supportive bra
questions.rationale: This is engorgement as milk comes in (days 2–4). With no fever or redness it isn't mastitis.

questions.stem: What is expected in the breasts on day 1 postpartum?
questions.rationale: Day 1: soft with colostrum. Days 2–4: heavier and fuller.

questions.stem: Why does she sit on the edge of the bed before getting up the first time?
questions.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is a normal postpartum cardiovascular change.

questions.stem: Exercises for diastasis recti:
options: Abdominal tightening, head lifts, pelvic tilts, Kegels
questions.rationale: These are the postpartum exercises on the slides.

questions.stem: Parents say, “If only we'd come in sooner.” Grief stage?
questions.rationale: Shock and disbelief, anger, guilt, sadness and depression, then gradual resolution.

questions.stem: After a stillbirth, the best nursing action is to:
options: Offer to let them hold the baby and prepare them for its appearance
Move them to a busy room
Say they can try again soon
questions.rationale: Also give privacy and mementos, ask about rituals, and refer to support groups.

questions.stem: Correct way to thaw frozen breast milk:
questions.rationale: Never microwave it. Discard warmed milk after 1–2 h.

questions.stem: Which feeding is dropped LAST when weaning?
questions.rationale: Drop one at a time, daytime first, favourite last.

questions.stem: At 2 weeks: fundus still palpable, lochia rubra, pelvic heaviness. Suspect:
questions.rationale: Subinvolution is a common cause of late PPH.

questions.stem: DIC after birth is:
options: Over-activated clotting that uses up clotting factors and causes uncontrolled bleeding
questions.rationale: DIC is the Thrombin T of the 4 T's.

questions.stem: Anticoagulant teaching includes:
options: Report nosebleeds, bruising or prolonged bleeding; use a soft toothbrush
questions.rationale: Also teach how to give the medication.

questions.stem: Who is MOST at risk for mastitis?
options: Cracked nipples and a poor latch
questions.rationale: Cracked nipples let bacteria in, and a poor latch leaves the breast full.

questions.stem: How do newborns mainly produce heat?
questions.rationale: Sweat glands don't work yet. Cold stress can cause hypoglycemia and respiratory distress.

questions.stem: Turn the head right: the right arm and leg extend. Which reflex?
questions.rationale: Tonic neck: the arm and leg on the side the head faces extend.

questions.stem: A breastfed baby is 3 days old. Expected wet diapers today?
questions.rationale: 1 on day 1, then add one per day, reaching 6–8 by day 5.

questions.stem: Newborn screening is best done at:
questions.rationale: It covers up to 40 conditions, including PKU, hypothyroidism, galactosemia and sickle cell.

questions.stem: A post-term baby born through meconium-stained fluid has grunting, retractions and rhonchi. Expect:
options: Meconium aspiration syndrome; tachypnea may last weeks
questions.rationale: MAS: respiratory distress, flaring, retractions, cyanosis, grunting, rales/rhonchi, tachypnea over 60.
